Review Body: No. This book has story after story of horrific trauma: war PTSD, rape, forced prostitution. Sorry for them but, mercifully, not me. I just have disappointments. At my very first visit with a Chinese acupuncturist, she asked what major life events happened the year before my first major knee problem. I shrugged my shoulders. She insisted. I said, “Oh! My absentee father died and my ex-boyfriend got married.” She said, “You are afraid to move forward! Knee problems come from not knowing how to move forward!” Then she gave me some homework and a life's worth of introspection. That’s what I wanted out of this book but didn’t get. I couldn’t stomach one more horrible story and all the scientific talk about experimentation, observations, and failed treatments. This book keeps coming up in articles that I read. He claims this kind of torture isn't something he supports yet he goes into further depth this "study" which validates it altogether. He claims this information helped him figure out important aspects of his work with humans.

2. He goes on and on about the wonders of pharmaceuticals in various chapters and so many times throughout you begin to think he was paid by the industry to write the book.

3. He doesn't really going into depth about how the body actually keeps the score and is much more focused on the various ways to treat- again, based on pharmaceuticals.

4. He mentions a women who was brutally raped at 16 and then continues the pattern with abusive men and blames it on that experience. Wrong. Whatever happened in her formative years is why she was in a that pattern- not because of a single experience.

5. He's an old school, pharmaceutical drug based type of doctor that believes in and relies on torturous animals experimentation to draw conclusions. The kind after Rockefeller's own heart. Not nearly enough about inner healing, alternative medicine, self-love, and modern ways to explain and approach how the body keeps score.

There is sympathetic talk of treatment of a vet who is a rapist, murderer, and domestic violence perpetrator in the first chapter. If you feel like you may be sensitive to casual talk of rape and murder, be aware that this is in the book right off the bat.

The conclusions at the end are that you need community, people to touch you, yoga, mindfulness and therapy. Don’t waste your time or money on this.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on March 13, 2022
Review Body: Disappointed to see that information aimed at individuals with trauma is interspersed with dark stories of trauma. It doesn't make sense to me - the anecdotes are more appropriate for a book that has a trigger warning saying it may not be suitable for those who have experienced trauma.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 25, 2022
Review Body: The author chose to describe many abusive incidents or accidents in graphic detail that are now forever in my mind causing me further pain and suffering with PTSD. If you are a visual person, do not read this book.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 16, 2022
Review Body: Do not recommend for survivors of SA! Tried to write a review already an Amazon hid it. How many other peoples bad views also didn’t make it through? This book is poorly written and can be very triggering for trauma survivors
